questions.question: What is the main output of a boilerplate detector?
options: A guarantee that the source HTML is safe to render
A decision about which page regions belong to the target document
A browser screenshot with all styles removed
A replacement for fetching and rendering the page
questions.explanation: Boilerplate detection classifies and reconstructs page regions for an extraction target. Acquisition, JavaScript rendering, sanitization, and downstream rendering remain separate responsibilities.

questions.question: A documentation table contains valuable facts but almost no full sentences. Which lesson does this illustrate?
options: Sentence count is a perfect content signal
One density rule can miss valid content shapes
Tables should always be removed as navigation
Only CSS classes should decide extraction
questions.explanation: Feature behavior depends on page shape. A sentence-heavy rule may work for articles while missing tables, code, captions, or other valid content.

questions.question: At a fixed labeled evaluation set, raising the keep threshold usually has which effect?
options: It keeps more blocks and can raise recall
It keeps fewer blocks, often raising precision while lowering recall
It makes precision and recall identical
It removes the need for representative fixtures
questions.explanation: A higher threshold accepts fewer candidates. That can remove false positives, but it can also turn lower-scoring true content into false negatives.

questions.question: Why should evaluation results be sliced by page type or template family?
options: A single aggregate score can hide severe failures on one content shape
Each page type requires a different programming language
Slicing guarantees perfect extraction
It prevents website templates from changing
questions.explanation: An aggregate can look healthy while forums, tables, galleries, or one publisher template fail badly. Slices expose where the policy needs a different feature, fallback, or route.

questions.question: A fetched HTML response does not contain text that a client-side script inserts later. What must happen before a DOM-only detector can classify that text?
options: Increase the link-density threshold
Obtain a representation in which the script-generated content exists, such as an allowed rendered DOM
Treat every empty block as main content
Run the quiz first
questions.explanation: An extractor cannot classify nodes absent from its input. Rendering may be needed for approved sources, but it adds browser cost, execution risk, and another failure boundary.

questions.question: Why must extracted HTML still be sanitized before being rendered in an application?
options: Content scoring removes all unsafe markup by definition
Main-content extraction and output sanitization solve different problems
Sanitization improves recall
It makes the original website trustworthy
questions.explanation: Selecting relevant nodes does not prove their markup is safe. Treat extracted HTML as untrusted input and apply context-appropriate sanitization and output controls.
